title: Medicine
hook: Luke the beloved physician, a Samaritan with oil and wine: Christians see healing by doctors as God's work too

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hospital hallway and a courtroom, and the hardest choices. Your line was every life counts. When one of those questions came up, what life did you hear underneath it? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

Hospitals carry some telling names. Good Samaritan. Mercy. Saint Luke's. You may have driven past one this year without a second thought. But that last name belongs to a man the New Testament names only in passing. In a greeting at the end of one of Paul's letters, he's called "Luke, the beloved physician." Tradition says this is the same Luke who wrote a Gospel and the book of Acts. A doctor, in other words, standing right in the middle of the early church's story, and nobody in it seems to think that's strange. Today: medicine.

Jesus himself reaches for the doctor when he describes his own work. Criticized for eating with sinners, he answers: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." He doesn't treat the physician as a rival to God. He uses the physician as the picture. Then there's the Good Samaritan, whose name ended up on hospitals too. Look at what he actually does on that road. He doesn't just feel sorry for the wounded man. He "bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine." That's first aid, the medicine of the day. And he doesn't stop there. He brings the man to an inn, pays, and tells the innkeeper, "Take care of him." Emergency care, then ongoing care, with the bill covered. One more text, the book of Sirach, sits in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the Apocrypha in some Protestant ones. It tells readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him, and it says the Lord brings medicines out of the earth. Put these together and you get a way of seeing medicine. When someone gets well under a surgeon's hands or a nurse's patience or a pharmacist's careful counting, Christians who see it this way don't call it God's work or the doctor's. They call it both. God heals, and very often God heals through hands. That's why prayer and medicine are allowed to sit in the same room.

Here's the practice: remember the hands. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one time someone helped you or someone you love get well. A doctor who explained things slowly. A nurse on a night shift. A pharmacist who caught a mistake. A parent with a bandage and a steady voice. Let one face come clear, and remember what their hands actually did. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that person by name. If you don't, just let yourself be grateful to them. The bell holds the time.
Medicine. For Christians who see it this way, the healing work of doctors, nurses and every careful hand, which they count as God's work too.

Your line: God heals through hands. Today, thank one person who has cared for your health, a doctor, a nurse, a pharmacist, in a message or face to face, and tell them one specific thing they did. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Christians pray for the sick and for those who treat them; churches run hospitals, clinics and nursing ministries, and some keep a feast of Saint Luke, when they remember doctors and pray for healers.

notes: The outline hook says Christians built hospitals; under the claims rule the script does not state that history, and only notes hospital names such as Good Samaritan, Mercy and Saint Luke's. howItsDone says churches run hospitals and clinics (a present-tense description); confirm or soften.
Lucan authorship of the Gospel and Acts is attributed to tradition, not stated as fact.

Sirach 38:1–4 paraphrased (honor the physician, the Lord created him, the Lord created medicines out of the earth). Canon status stated as: in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, among the Apocrypha in some Protestant Bibles. Confirm.
howItsDone mentions a feast of Saint Luke kept by some churches; confirm wording.
Matthew 9:12 context (eating with publicans and sinners) summarized as 'criticized for eating with sinners'; the critics (Pharisees in 9:11) are not named, to avoid a foil.

Editor: Luke is named in several letters but called a physician only in Colossians 4:14, so the hook now says that; 'all those hospitals' softened; the teach and myth no longer imply the Samaritan prayed (Luke 10 does not say so); 'carries' corrected to 'brings' (he set him on his own beast).
